themes.topic: Human wisdom as knowing one's own ignorance

mentions.quote: I am wiser than this man; for neither of us really knows anything fine and good, but this man thinks he knows something when he does not, whereas I, as I do not know anything, do not think I do either
Human wisdom is of little or no value. And it appears that he does not really say this of Socrates, but merely uses my name, and makes me an example
For no one knows whether death be not even the greatest of all blessings to man, but they fear it as if they knew that it is the greatest of evils

themes.justification: The Socratic discovery that true human wisdom consists in awareness of one's own ignorance is the central epistemic argument developed across the oracle narrative and the cross-examination of Meletus.

themes.topic: The philosophical mission as divine vocation

mentions.quote: I am still even now going about and searching and investigating at the god's behest anyone, whether citizen or foreigner, who I think is wise
the god gave me a station, as I believed and understood, with orders to spend my life in philosophy and in examining myself and others
I think the god fastened me upon the city in some such capacity, and I go about arousing, and urging and reproaching each one of you

themes.justification: Socrates consistently frames his philosophical activity not as personal choice but as a divine assignment derived from the Delphic oracle, making piety and mission inseparable.

themes.topic: The tension between obedience to divine and civic authority

mentions.quote: Men of Athens, I respect and love you, but I shall obey the god rather than you
A man who really fights for the right, if he is to preserve his life for even a little while, must be a private citizen, not a public man
I thought I must run the risk to the end with law and justice on my side, rather than join with you when your wishes were unjust

themes.justification: The passage repeatedly raises the implicit conflict between the demands of the polis (laws, democratic assembly, tyrants) and the demands of the god, without making it a formal philosophical argument.

themes.topic: Rhetoric, truth, and the ethics of speech

mentions.quote: they call him a clever speaker who speaks the truth; for if this is what they mean, I would agree that I am an orator—not after their fashion
you shall hear from me nothing but the truth
for that is the virtue of a judge, and an orator's virtue is to speak the truth
we ought to inform and convince him. For the judge is not here to grant favors in matters of justice, but to give judgement

themes.justification: The distinction between ornate courtroom rhetoric and plain truth-telling frames the entire speech and constitutes a sustained implicit argument about what legitimate persuasion looks like.

themes.topic: The examined life and the care of the soul

mentions.quote: I tell you that virtue does not come from money, but from virtue comes money and all other good things to man, both to the individual and to the state
to talk every day about virtue and the other things about which you hear me talking and examining myself and others is the greatest good to man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living
I tried to persuade each of you to care for himself and his own perfection in goodness and wisdom rather than for any of his belongings

themes.justification: The care of the soul over external goods and the value of self-examination are recurring normative claims that define Socrates' account of his own beneficial service to Athens.

themes.topic: Death, courage, and the fear of the unknown

mentions.quote: For to fear death, gentlemen, is nothing else than to think one is wise when one is not; for it is thinking one knows what one does not know

wherever a man stations himself, thinking it is best to be there, or is stationed by his commander, there he must remain and run his risks, considering neither death nor any other thing more than disgrace

the state of death is one of two things: either it is virtually nothingness, so that the dead has no consciousness of anything, or it is, as people say, a change and migration of the soul from this to another place

themes.justification: The proper philosophical attitude toward death — neither fearing it nor craving it but remaining open to its unknown nature — is a sustained theme culminating in the two-hypothesis analysis of death in p-3b58fe.

themes.topic: The corruption of reputation and popular prejudice

mentions.quote: many accusers have risen up against me before you, who have been speaking for a long time, many years already, and saying nothing true
I fear them more than Anytus and the rest
many enmities have arisen against me, and such as are most harsh and grievous, so that many prejudices have resulted from them and I am called a wise man

great hatred has arisen against me and in the minds of many persons. And this it is which will cause my condemnation, if it is to cause it, not Meletus or Anytus, but the prejudice and dislike of the many

themes.justification: Socrates consistently distinguishes the formal legal accusation from the older, deeper popular prejudice that he regards as the real cause of his danger, making the sociology of reputation a central analytical concern.

themes.topic: True and false teaching: sophists versus philosophy

mentions.quote: if one might be able to teach people, as Gorgias of Leontini and Prodicus of Ceos and Hippias of Elis are
that is not true either

Evenus, he said, Socrates, from Paros, five minae. And I called Evenus blessed, if he really had this art and taught so reasonably. I myself should be vain and put on airs, if I understood these things
I was never any one's teacher. If any one, whether young or old, wishes to hear me speaking and pursuing my mission, I have never objected

themes.justification: Socrates explicitly contrasts the paid sophistic model of teaching virtue with his own unpaid practice of philosophical questioning, making the distinction between sophistry and philosophy a background theme throughout.

mentions.quote: something divine and spiritual comes to me, the very thing which Meletus ridiculed in his indictment. I have had this from my childhood; it is a sort of voice that comes to me, and when it comes it always holds me back from what I am thinking of doing, but never urges me forward

the customary prophetic monitor always spoke to me very frequently and opposed me even in very small matters, if I was going to do anything I should not; but now, as you yourselves see, this thing which might be thought, and is generally considered, the greatest of evils has come upon me; but the divine sign did not oppose me

themes.justification: The daimonion — the inner divine voice — is a recurring motif explicitly named and explained by Socrates, functioning as personal moral guidance distinct from both the oracle and conventional piety.

themes.topic: Justice, injustice, and the moral limits of self-preservation

mentions.quote: I do know that it is evil and disgraceful to do wrong and to disobey him who is better than I, whether he be god or man
I thought I must run the risk to the end with law and justice on my side, rather than join with you when your wishes were unjust, through fear of imprisonment or death
it is not hard to escape death; it is much harder to escape wickedness, for that runs faster than death

themes.justification: The implicit philosophical claim running through the Leon episode, the Achilles parallel, and the closing prophecy is that moral integrity constitutes a higher obligation than self-preservation — a Socratic axiom stated most starkly in p-92dd99.

citations.quote: For you yourselves saw these things in Aristophanes' comedy, a Socrates being carried about there, proclaiming that he was treading on air and uttering a vast deal of other nonsense, about which I know nothing, either much or little
citations.justification: Socrates explicitly names Aristophanes' comedy as the source of the false popular image of him as a natural philosopher, and distances himself from its portrayal.

citations.quote: the books of Anaxagoras the Clazomenian are full of such utterances? And forsooth the youth learn these doctrines from me, which they can buy sometimes (if the price is high) for a drachma in the orchestra
citations.justification: Socrates cites the widely available books of Anaxagoras to refute Meletus's charge that Socrates teaches the sun is a stone and the moon earth — those doctrines belong to Anaxagoras, not Socrates.

citations.quote: Straightway may I die, after doing vengeance upon the wrongdoer, that I may not stay here, jeered at beside the curved ships, a burden of the earth
citations.justification: Socrates quotes the Achilles speech — attributable to the Iliad — as an authoritative model of preferring honourable death to survival in disgrace, directly parallel to his own situation.

citations.cited_work: Homeric tradition / Odyssey or related epics (implied)
citations.quote: I am, as Homer has it, not born of an oak or a rock, but of human parents
citations.justification: Socrates explicitly names Homer as the source of the phrase, using it as an authoritative literary expression to assert his ordinary human origins and therefore his possession of family.
